# 22 — The Crew: The Quest for Planet Nine

**Built and playing** — `game/games/the_crew.json`, generated by
`tools/make_the_crew.py`, tested by `tests/integration/the_crew.lua`. Four seats,
the full trick, the task draft, the radio token and both instant-loss triggers.

**Left:** the order tokens (`1`–`5`, `Ω`, `›`/`››`), which want a small authored
graph and a fourth loss check; the printed fifty missions, replaced here by an
opening overlay asking how many tasks the crew wants; three and five players,
which only the seat list and the rect arithmetic would have to agree about; and
the two-player JARVIS variant, which is a different game.

One deliberate deviation: the rulebook allows the radio *before* a trick and
never during one, and here it is usable on your own turn until you play into the
middle. That keeps every decision the token has — which card, which claim, which
trick — at the cost of letting a later seat speak having seen the cards played.

## The one gap, and both halves of it

The research checked eighteen rules and found **one** with no answer: *the trick
winner becomes the next active seat*. That verdict held to the letter — everything
downstream turned out to be content, including the two expected to be hard.

**`@owner_of.<scope>` reads it.** `score@owner_of.target` is the score of whoever
owns the card the player chose; alone, `@owner_of` is the acting card's own seat,
which no card could name before. Four decisions:

- **It answers with the seat's *card*, not a key**, because a scope's answer is
  entities everywhere else — and the card's `def_key` is the seat key, so the
  writing half reads it back off the same answer.
- **It uses `predicate.seat_of`, not `tags.owner_of`**, so the scope and the
  owner words can never disagree about whose a card is, and a seat card asked
  about itself answers itself rather than nobody.
- **An owner word means whichever side of the prefix it stands on** — inside it
  picks the cards, before it it filters the seats that come back. Each word sits
  beside what it is about, so neither reading has to be remembered.
- **Each seat answers once** however many cards it owns. A seat counted per card
  would pay a player twice for holding two pieces.

**`set_active_seat:<scope>` writes it**, as an ordinary action, so cards, zones
and phases all reach it. The scope names cards and the seat is whose they are,
through the same `seat_of` — so `set_active_seat:target` and
`set_active_seat:owner_of.target` say the same thing about an ordinary card. Two
seats is refused; none is not, because the trick is not won until somebody wins
it. A handover ends the undo history, as the end of a turn does.

It needed nothing from the network: the turn lives on the injected system card,
which is in the snapshot with everything else.

**Not built:** `"seat": "owner_of:<scope>"` as a routing spelling. The action
covers the trick winner from inside the phase that scores it, and nothing else
asked.

## What building it found

### The clamp at one exists after all

[23](23-splendor.md) closed by saying a clamp anywhere *but* at zero was still
missing. It is not — a floor at zero gives both halves:

```
min(a, k) = a - max(0, a - k)
```

Three actions and one scratch number with `min: 0`. **The floor is the only
operator the grammar has, and it is enough for both directions.**

**And Tough does not even need that much.** [18](18-legends-of-runeterra.md)
reads the rule as `min(1, damage)`, concludes it cannot be written, and ships an
approximation that *heals* against a zero-power source. But the rule is "reduce
incoming damage by 1, never below 0", which is `max(0, a - b)` and has been
available since stats had floors. It looked impossible because the subtraction
was attempted on the way *out*, after the damage had landed. On a scratch number
on the way in it is three ordinary lines. 18 was right that a replacement effect
is the general answer and wrong that this case needs one.

### Equality is two clamped subtractions, so a branch is a multiplication

`|a - b|` has no spelling and does not need one: subtract each way with a floor
of zero, take both from 1, and what is left is 1 exactly when they were equal.
That flag then *multiplies* the value, which is how "what would this card win
with" is written without a branch. **`max:` was never the missing piece** — the
led suit is a *number* the cards compare themselves against, not a scope name to
be chosen between, so the one-clause-per-suit the analysis expected was none.

### A tag cannot see a hand, so the commander is asked seat by seat

`count:<tag>` searches grid zones only, so no tag scope reaches a hand, and
"whose hand holds this card" is exactly that question. It is asked once per seat,
of the seat itself — `card:<key>@mine.hand` works because a *zone* scope is not
restricted to grids, only a *tag* scope is — and the answer is a stat on the seat
card with `commander` a computed tag over it. Every later rule names the
commander in one word.

Two idioms fall out and both are worth keeping: *narrow with the zone and count
the tag*, and *walk the seats to write a stat, then make the answer a computed
tag*. [06](06-schema-and-types.md)'s `@everywhere` did not retire the second: it
answers *how many, anywhere*, not *whose*.

**The walk is also the only way to deal.** There is no word for "every seat in
turn" outside a phase, and `seat: "next"` is ignored on an `automatic` one, so a
three-way deal is three pairs of actions. Fine at four seats, clumsy at five.

### A card is born owned by where it was created

`cards.create` stamps `owner` from the zone a card is made in. The Crew deals
from one shared deck, so every card is unowned, and while it sits in a hand
`owner_of` falls back to the hand's seat. **That fallback evaporates the instant
the card is played into the shared trick** — and "whose is the winning card" is
the whole game. One word on every card's `play` fixes it:
`set_owner:self:mine`.

The alternative the research proposed — a `per_seat` trick zone — does not
survive contact with `activate_zone`, which resolves its argument to exactly one
zone. A trick weighed as a whole has to be one zone, so ownership has to be said.

### `activate_zone` runs a card's whole ability list

The winner needs each card's `contend` (its own business) and then `best` (the
trick's), and a card cannot compute the second from the first in one sweep. There
is no way to run *one* of a card's abilities, so the same ability runs twice with
the phase-level line between. The ability is idempotent, so the first pass's
output is garbage nobody reads. Cheap and honest, and it kept the whole
calculation on one tag.

### A grid zone never drew its label

Found by looking rather than by testing. Not this game's bug: LoR's `bench`,
Splendor's `nobles` and its `supply` had all named themselves since they shipped
and drawn nothing. Fixed, laid down before the cards so an empty row says what it
is waiting for.

### The radio needed five things, and none was about trick-taking

- **`ends_when`, so saying something is not spending your turn.** `ends_after`
  counts plays and cannot tell one from another.
- **A phase's `zone` as a list.** The open hand is a second place to play from.
- **`min:`**, beside `sum:` and `max:`. It only sees cards that carry the stat,
  which is the whole trick: give a pink card a `v_pink` and no other card one,
  and `min:v_pink@mine.hand` is *the lowest pink I hold* — a question no scope
  can ask, because a tag reads grid zones only.
- **`face_up` on a hand.**
- **An ability that reaches nothing is not offered.** The rule existed for
  `moves` only; the radio has twelve abilities and a hand answers two or three.

Two things fell out. **"Only" is the other two agreeing**: an ability takes no
`needs`, so `count:pink@mine.hand == 1` had nowhere to go — and it was not
needed, because `max:v_pink@mine.hand <= min:v_pink@mine.hand` is *I hold exactly
one pink* and is the better sentence. (That an ability cannot carry a `needs` is
still a hole; it just was not this one's.) And **the escape hatch was per-zone,
which two hands made wrong**: a lone gated card in the open hand would always
open it, which is follow-suit quietly switching itself off. It asks about every
zone the phase allows now.

### The table has four sides, and the engine owns two corners

The first layout stacked three seats down the left and read as a list rather than
a table. Four round a rectangle is both the commoner game and the clearer
picture: two hands along the top, two along the bottom in reverse, so **the seat
that follows you is the one to your left on screen**. Four also divides forty, so
the odd fourteenth card three seats leave in somebody's hand is gone.

Two rectangles are not the game's to use, both learnt by drawing them: **the HUD
writes into the top right** and **the event log into the bottom left**. Nothing
in `zones()` reaches into either.

## One correction from the research

"Win exactly N tricks", "win no tricks" and the rest are **not** in the 36-card
task deck, which expresses exactly one shape — *win the trick containing this
card*, optionally sequenced by an order token. The rest is per-mission rule text
printed in the logbook. Both systems are real and
[the_crew/rules.md](the_crew/rules.md) covers both.
